name: Karl Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What do you do on a normal shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Karl, 58, and I run a press brake that folds steel panels for kitchen appliances. I finished secondary school and moved to this machine from loading six months ago; I still ask the setter to check a new fold angle before I press a production sheet. My hands find a bent flange faster than any screen does.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do pay, family and new technology fit into your week?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Mei works at a clinic reception, and our grown children live on their own. This factory pays above the usual operator rate for late shifts, we have about fourteen months of expenses saved, and several other metal shops advertise nearby. I use AI every day to search the machine manual and turn rough shift notes into a clear log, but I verify dimensions from the drawing and the actual panel. Retirement is near enough to discuss, though we have not set a date or checked an income figure against household costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the shop that quicker purchasing emails are fine if somebody still measures the folded panel against the drawing. I would keep the setter's first-piece signoff before running the batch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our late-shift rate covers the bills and the fourteen-month reserve means a slow order week would not break us. Office AI alone does not remove the press brake or my hands at it. I am junior on this machine, so I want the first piece right before anyone celebrates an instant schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would run the press brake with the setter checking new angles and keep logging defects with the AI note tool I already use every day. If we have a full paid month after bills, Mei and I would put a new slice of that wage into savings, separate from the fourteen months already there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A faster order email is useful, but my wage still comes from panels that fit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened with the first piece on your last new batch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cabinet side sprung back a little, so the setter changed the angle and we measured it again. We did not send twenty bad panels through because the job card was typed quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your daily AI use look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I search a manual fault code and clean up my shift notes; I do that most days. I do not let a chat answer pick a bend angle or clear a machine fault without the setter and a physical check.

say: I would welcome **faster purchasing emails** if first-piece signoff stays.
The **panel drawing** still sets the measured fold.
think: The **late-shift wage** and fourteen-month reserve currently cover a slow week.
Office AI does not yet replace my **physical press work**.
do: **Keep** running the press brake with setter checks and daily AI logs.
**Save** new wages from full paid months after household bills.
feel: **Calm** because the current work and household income remain sound.
S0.quote: We did not send twenty bad panels through because the job card was typed quickly.
fieldNote: His **junior standing** is clear from the setter's first-piece signoff, despite his above-usual shift rate.
His **daily AI use** searches manuals and tidies notes; new savings would come only from future paid wages.

steps.text: Keep operating brake with setter signoff and daily AI shift logs
Save additional wages after bills from full paid months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say software can reorder sheet stock long before a robot can line up a warped panel. If management wants a camera on our brake, I would ask for a guarded trial and the proposed shift roster together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like new tools, but a tidy plan could let the plant merge late shifts and take away the rate that makes my pay high. We could absorb a short spell from savings and Mei's wage, but I would not call a permanent lower rate harmless. My daily AI manual searches are no substitute for learning a new brake control properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the proposed roster with my last four pay slips and ask the setter for a paid guarded trial of the new AI bend-check screen. If the trial is offered, I would practice marking good and bad scrap bends against the drawing before using it on a customer panel. If my paid late hours actually fall, I would apply to posted nearby metal-machine jobs only when the base pay after travel, safe duties and shift hours meet our monthly costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a real cut to my late-shift pay, even though I want to test the camera. I can be curious and still read a wage slip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a useful camera test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use a deliberately short fold, a good fold and a warped sheet on a scrap run. The setter should watch the guarded machine while I compare every screen mark with a caliper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change shops immediately?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would first see whether the posted roster actually cuts my hours, then compare genuine vacancies by base pay after travel. A higher advertised bonus can disappear if the late shift is not guaranteed.

say: I would ask for the **new roster** beside any camera proposal.
A **guarded scrap trial** should compare screen marks with measurements.
think: Merged late shifts could take away my **above-usual pay**.
Fourteen months **saved** buys time but cannot restore a permanently lower rate.
do: **Compare** the proposed roster with four actual pay slips.
**Learn** the new AI bend-check screen on offered paid guarded scrap runs.
**Apply** after actual cuts to posted safe nearby machine jobs at bill-covering net wages.
feel: **Anxious** about plausible late-rate loss while open to a safe camera trial.
S1.quote: I can be curious and still read a wage slip.
fieldNote: His **new AI learning** means active bend-check practice on paid guarded scrap; routine daily manual searches are existing use.
A **job switch** follows actual hours lost and posted safe work whose base wage after travel covers household costs.

steps.text: Compare proposed late roster with four pay slips

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Mei that AGI might plan orders in 2028, while robots able to lift and bend the actual sheets arrive around 2031. I would ask our plant which paid operator posts would remain when the robot brake goes in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 at the robot date, with only six months on this brake now and no senior claim to a retained post. I expect most manual press shifts to vanish, including mine, and the higher late rate would be hard to replace. Fourteen months saved is a runway, but I have begun waking at night wondering whether another shop would pay enough after travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would postpone replacing the bathroom fittings and keep that money for household bills. I would take a recognised press-maintenance course only if a funded place gives paid time, supervised lockout practice and a machine I can safely work on. After qualifying, if my shifts fall, I would apply to posted safe local maintenance jobs only if their base pay after travel and shift pattern cover costs; if no suitable course place appears, I would search posted local machine jobs on those same terms while keeping paid shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I could learn the new equipment, but a machine that removes my paid shift before a real job opens is a serious problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the maintenance course have to teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would isolate the brake, test that it cannot move, and diagnose a bend sensor with a trainer at my side. A video certificate would not make me safe beside a moving ram.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not retire at 63?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mei and I have not checked any written retirement income against housing, food and health expenses. I would stop paid work only if that full calculation covers us. A birthday by itself does not pay for dinner.

say: I would separate **2028 order AGI** from physical brake robots around 2031.
The plant should show **remaining paid posts** before installing a robot brake.
think: At **63**, my junior status gives me no retained-job guarantee.
Expected press-shift loss threatens the **higher late rate** despite fourteen months saved.
do: **Postpone** bathroom spending to protect cash for bills.
**Train** only in funded paid recognised maintenance with supervised safe lockout practice.
**Apply** after cuts to posted safe maintenance if qualified, otherwise machine work, at viable net pay.
feel: **Alarmed** by likely major shift loss and waking at night over income.
S2.quote: A birthday by itself does not pay for dinner.
fieldNote: He expects **physical robot displacement** around 2031 rather than an immediate loss from office planning AGI.
Both **job searches** require real safe local postings, workable wages after travel and shift fit.

steps.text: Postpone bathroom fittings and hold money for household bills
Take recognised maintenance course only with funded paid supervised lockout place
Apply after cuts to posted safe local maintenance if qualified and net pay fits
Search posted safe local machine jobs if no course, with bill-covering net pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew AGI could plan metal orders in 2031 while capable robots that feed and bend sheets arrive around 2034. Five years is enough to ask which maintenance qualification nearby plants actually put in their job ads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 66 then. Mei and I might retire before a robot takes this shift, but we have not measured written income against housing and medical costs, so I cannot count on that. I learn controls quickly, yet I am still a junior brake operator and cannot assume the plant will give me a specialist post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would save a fresh part of each full month's late-rate wages after expenses and ask two nearby plants which maintenance credential their posted jobs accept. I would enrol only if the accepted course offers a funded place, paid release from shifts and supervised lockout practice on a guarded machine. If I pass and paid hours fall, I would apply to posted safe local maintenance jobs only if base pay after travel and shifts cover our bills; if no place opens, I would search posted machine jobs on the same pay and safety terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about whether we still need this wage at 66. The extra time would let me test a real route before the old shift shrinks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide whether the credential is useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would match its name to actual vacancies at the two metal shops and ask whether supervised lockout is part of the course. If neither plant accepts it, I would keep the wage and look for a different offered place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the new savings be your existing fourteen months?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Fourteen months of household expenses are already saved. I mean putting a new amount from future full paid shifts away after rent, food and travel.

A **five-year interval** gives time to test a safe course route.
think: At **66**, retirement may work only if written income covers costs.
My **junior press skill** is no guarantee of a specialist job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI may plan appliance orders in 2036, while capable robots reach the physical press around 2039. We can use the long interval to check real retirement figures and the work still offered locally.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 71 when those robots arrive, if I am still working. Our high current rate, Mei's income and fourteen-month reserve make our bills safe now, but retirement depends on written income after housing and health costs. I would not assume an age brings a payment we have not checked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking paid safe press shifts and ask for written retirement-income estimates and a household cost list this year. If we decide I still need a wage, I would take an accepted maintenance course only with funded fees, paid release and supervised lockout practice. If I remain at work after 2036 and shifts fall, I would apply to posted safe nearby machine or maintenance jobs only if the base pay after travel and shift times cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about an unmeasured far-off decision, though this month's household income is secure. I prefer a cost sheet with numbers to a confident retirement guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who will do the household arithmetic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mei and I will put the written estimates beside rent, food, transport and likely health costs. Our grown children have their own bills; I will not count their income as ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if a maintenance course is not offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would continue paid safe press work while it is there, then check actual posted machine vacancies if hours fall. A course title without a funded place does not move a panel or pay our rent.

Written **retirement figures** must be compared with real household costs.

Current **higher pay** and fourteen months saved secure the near term.

feel: **Uneasy** about distant retirement arithmetic while current bills remain secure.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 AGI picture worries me most because a capable brake robot around 2031 could remove my late-rate shift while I still need its wage. A funded safe maintenance place, written shift dates and posted local jobs at enough pay after travel would help. I would compare retirement income with costs before treating it as an escape.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who is blamed when a panel is bent wrong after the software says it is fine. I would rather have a measured first piece and a setter's initials than a fast log describing scrap beautifully.

headlineQuote: I would rather have a measured first piece and a setter's initials than a fast log describing scrap beautifully.
portrait: **Karl**, 58, is a junior press-brake operator with secondary education, still learning steel-panel settings from a setter.
He and his **wife Mei** have grown children, fourteen months of expenses saved and higher late-shift pay; several metal shops are nearby.
He uses **AI daily** for manuals and shift notes, but checks machine dimensions against drawings and real first pieces.
He is curious about new controls yet expects **2031 robots** to threaten his paid shift; retirement needs written income after household costs.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could precede physical brake robots around 2031, removing his higher paid late shifts.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **funded supervised maintenance training**, dated shift plans, posted safe local jobs with adequate net pay and written retirement figures.
